sections.text:
1 Achmetis hic prooemium et capitula nonnulla introductionis protulimus quo
facilius de indole operis ad hunc diem ignoti iudicetur. An scriptor eius idem sit
atque Ἀχμὲτ υἱὸς Σερεὶμ ὁ ὀνειροκρίτης τοῦ πρώτου συμβούλου Μαμοῦν, cuius
onirocritica edidit Rigaltius (Paris 1603), incertum est, veri tamen non est simile,
nam Achmet ille anno circiter 820 p. C. n. florebat (Krumbacher, Gesch. Byz.
Lit., p. 630, ed. 2; Ruelle, Rev. ét. gr., VII, p. 305), hi libri autem apotelesmatici
non ante saeculum decimum compositi esse videntur, cum plura ex Apomasare,
anno 885 p. C. n. mortuo, contineant. Fortasse de Abu Dja'afar Ahmed ben Jusuf
ben Ibrahim, viro non Persa sed Aegyptio, qui circa ann. 945 mortuus est, cogitan-
dum (Steinschneider, Hebräische Uebersetz. des Mittelalters, § 326, p. 326). At vide
ne opus vel ex toto vel partim a falsario inlustri astrologo suppositum sit, nam qui
haec consarcinavit Hephaestionem Thebanum (supra, p. 13, n. 1) expilavit. — Ach-
metis libri astrologici in codicibus plurifariam inveniuntur e. g. in Angelicano 29,
saec. XIII, f. 181v ss. (Studi italiani di fil., IV, cod. 62), et in cod. Palatino
Vatic. 312, f. 86-115.
F. C.
sections.en:
1 We have brought forward here the preface and some chapters of the introduction of Achmet so that
the nature of the work, unknown to this day, may be more easily judged. Whether its writer is the same
as Ἀχμὲτ υἱὸς Σερεὶμ ὁ ὀνειροκρίτης τοῦ πρώτου συμβούλου Μαμοῦν ('Achmet son of Sereim the dream-interpreter of the first counselor Mamoun'), whose
dream-interpretations Rigaltius edited (Paris 1603), is uncertain, but it is not likely,
for that Achmet flourished around the year 820 A.D. (Krumbacher, Gesch. Byz.
Lit., p. 630, ed. 2; Ruelle, Rev. ét. gr., VII, p. 305), but these apotelesmatic books
seem to have been composed not before the tenth century, since they contain many things from Apomasar,
who died in the year 885 A.D. Perhaps Abu Dja'afar Ahmed ben Jusuf
ben Ibrahim, a man not Persian but Egyptian, who died around the year 945, should be thought of
(Steinschneider, Hebräische Uebersetz. des Mittelalters, § 326, p. 326). But see
whether the work was either wholly or partly substituted by a forger for the illustrious astrologer, for he who
patched these things together plundered Hephaestion of Thebes (above, p. 13, n. 1). — Achmet's
astrological books are found in many places in codices, e.g. in Angelicanus 29,
13th cent., f. 181v ff. (Studi italiani di fil., IV, cod. 62), and in cod. Palatinus
Vatic. 312, f. 86-115.
[F. C.]

summary.headline: Achmet’s Astrological Introduction
summary.text: Achmet’s “Introduction and Foundation to Astrology,” beginning with its Persian sources, compilation from ancient books, and division into four books. The opening proem presents astrology as grounded in knowledge of the stars, their motions, positions, and prediction.
